title: How to Read the Bible With Young Children
excerpt: You do not need a curriculum or a clever method. You need to open the book, read a little, and let your children watch you take it seriously.
body:
Parents freeze at the thought of reading the Bible with small children. They worry they will explain it wrong, that the hard parts will confuse, that they themselves do not know enough. So they outsource it to a video or a Sunday program and never open the book at home. The children grow up knowing the Bible is a thing other people handle, not a book their own family lives inside.

The fear is misplaced. You are not required to be a scholar. You are required to be a parent who opens the book. Deuteronomy 6 does not say teach diligently once you have a seminary degree. It says teach diligently, sitting in your house, walking on the road, the ordinary parent in the ordinary day. The qualification is presence, not expertise.

## Start with story, because the Bible is mostly story

The Bible is not first a rulebook or a theology text. It is overwhelmingly a story, the long account of what God has done, and children are built for story. Begin where the story is strongest. Creation. Noah. Abraham. Joseph. The exodus. David. And above all the Gospels, the life of Jesus told plainly.

A good illustrated story Bible is a fine on-ramp for the very young, as long as it stays close to the text and does not flatten everything into a moral lesson. But move to the real Bible sooner than you think. A five-year-old can follow a paragraph of Mark read slowly. Do not underestimate what a child can hold.

## Read short, read often

The instinct is to read a long passage and explain everything. Resist it. Read a few verses. A single scene. Then stop while attention is still alive. It is far better to read five verses every day than three chapters once a month and burn everyone out. Frequency forms a child. Length does not.

Keep it at a fixed point in the day, riding on a habit you already have. The end of breakfast. The start of bedtime. Children settle into rhythms, and the rhythm carries the practice through the days when no one feels like it.

## Ask, do not lecture

After you read, do not deliver a sermon. Ask. "What happened in that story?" "What did Jesus do?" "How do you think the man felt?" Let the children retell it in their own words, which is how they make it theirs. Their answers will be strange and wrong and wonderful, and you correct gently and let them keep talking.

Then point, once, to Jesus. Almost every story is going somewhere, and where it is going is the rescue God is working through his Son. "God kept his promise to Abraham, and the biggest promise was Jesus." One sentence. Do not over-spiritualize a battle scene or wring a lesson out of every detail. Let the story be a story. The big picture forms over years, not in one sitting.

## Do not skip the hard parts forever

The Bible has darkness in it. People die. There is sin and judgment and a cross. You will moderate what you read to a three-year-old, of course. But do not raise children on a sanitized Bible where nothing is ever at stake, because they will grow up and find the real one and feel they were lied to. Let the difficulty in slowly, in proportion to their age. A child who learns that the Bible is honest about a broken world will trust it later when their own world breaks.

I have softened passages to the point of dishonesty, eager to keep things pleasant. The children sensed the gap. Honesty, even hard honesty, builds more trust than a comfortable fiction ever will.

## Let them see it matters to you

The deepest teaching is not in the words you say about the text. It is in the way your children watch you receive it. If you open the Bible distracted, half-present, treating it as a chore to clear, they learn that it is a chore. If you open it as a man or woman who needs it, who is fed by it, who is sometimes stopped by it, they learn that this book is alive. You cannot fake this, and you do not have to. Let them catch you needing it.

## This week

Pick one Gospel, Mark is short and fast, and read the first scene aloud to your young children today. A few verses, no more. Ask them what happened. Let them tell it back. Say one sentence about Jesus. Tomorrow, read the next scene. Keep going through the book, a little each day, attached to a meal you already share.

You are not running a class. You are letting your children grow up inside a book, the way a person grows up inside a home, until its rooms are familiar and they could find their way in the dark.
